questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to find professors and researchers doing work in my areas of interest.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Everything was fairly easy in that regard. Main issue was signing up for Master's level courses from a university-wide exchange spot, as that is an extremely involved and non-obvious process at University of Washington side

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received a welcome tour around the campus from the US side of the exchange. It was also fairly easy to contact the study abroad department on the US side.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: We could sign up for dorms or apartments

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No cooking facilities were available in the dorm (McMahon Hall). There was a very expensive meal plan at the university, which was mandatory if you chose to stay at the dorm (you would not get your meal plan funds back if you did not use them).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Best avoid it if you can, but of course its very hard to find a different apartment across timezones. The dorms have a very strict guest policy so you will not be able to have friends over for longer than 3 days during one semester.

Buy the cheapest meal plan that you are forced into, then cook for yourself at the dorm (you can buy a fridge from the Housing Foundation and order smth like kettles and toasters off Amazon). 

Avoid chicken and egg products, as they are known to be of poor quality and cause salmonella frequently.

Other groceries are fine, just dont buy at the Campus stores, since they are way overpriced.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's there but its very expensive. Even the US students usually move off campus after their first year.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
It's relatively easy to sign up for bachelors-level (undergrad) courses, as long as you write to the teacher explaining how you fulfill the prerequisites from the courses you already took elsewhere.

Registering for anything Masters (400 and 500 level) is borderline impossible.

Professors unfortunately have very little say in who gets admited - you are the last in the administrative priority list and any UW student will get in before you every time.

You have to fill out special forms for every single one - sending emails to professors is not enough.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We could book or pop into a course advisor's office. They are very helpful about figuring out the signup process in general, but dont expect them to make any exceptions in terms of where and when you can signup for courses (thats part of the behind the scenes process)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was lucky enough to find a good research opportunity that I managed to sign up for. If not for that, I would mostly be forced into Bachelor level courses. I managed to get into one strictly Masters level course through the form application I mentioned earlier.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Start filling out forms early. Dont bother writing emails to professors until you get some sort of a response from the form.

If you manage to find a professor looking for researchers, sign up - you can get credits for that. The research work is on an exceptionally high level in terms of what you can learn and contribute to.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
As explained in the student advice above - I took one Masters level class in Compilers which was extremely pragmatic, well-explained and useful, although the workload was quite high.

I took one Leadership class from Bachelor's level.

Rest of my time I did research with PhD students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There is way more workload expected per credit (even if you translate into ECTS). Its much less flexible - at UCPH I was mostly doing projects and learning through those, whilst at UW you will have more traditional homework.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer: Research and Reading;

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Research at UW is extremely good. My lab mates were very competent PhD students, always on top of the latest publications.

Introduction to Compiler Construction was a very informative course. All theory was explained in terms of the homeworks we were doing (which were all part of a single larger project). All necessary knowledge was explained as needed (e.x. you dont have to be a master at Assembly, as all the necessary parts were re-introduced for the project).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were social events happening nearly every day. There is a gym-membership included in Housing Foundation Card (the meal plan). All the sports facilities are exceptional. There are all sorts of sports available (e.x. kayaking, archery, soccer, basketball, swimming)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Gym is very good. Sign up for archery class (good as a social event), or any other class you are interested in - you will definitely find your favorites.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Try flying around the West Coast if you can afford it. Las Vegas, Vancouver, Texas are all great destinations. There is also a hiking club and student clubs available for socializing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy, had to wrap my mind around undisclosed sales taxes and tipping culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sign up for your favorite spot and just pick one of the many widely advertised events that happen constantly.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Mostly around the crime rate. There is a lot of crime and drug addicts on the streets. You have to be very careful where you go, especially at night (but unfortunately violent crime also happens in broad daylight). Police will not come, the ambulance most likely neither.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
People are extremely chatty and open. You can strike up a conversation with anybody on the street at any time - thats the norm, expect others to do the same :)

You will easily find people to hang out with at bars and other social gatherings.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get involved in some organized activities to make friends.

Find researchers and professors that are looking for more people - you are no cost to them and will profit immensely from the opportunity.

Go out and explore the country - just be careful around the drug addicts in cities.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get Amazon Prime - you will get everything you need for day-to-day living there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting bright like-minded people who mentored me academically and exploring the beautiful nature of the US.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Registering for classes at an appropriate level.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
